div.p: This research investigates the capability of a multiprocessor system in guaranteeing the execution of critical tasks and determines the cause of deadline failures. By implementing a real-time application using an INMOS transputer and Occam language, we were able to distribute required tasks among the processors and determine their CPUs usage. We evaluated the performance of the system in terms of the number of guaranteed critical and non-critical tasks, arrival rates, and conflicting deadlines.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The intent of this research is to design and implement a multi-robotics system and determine the eause of deadline failures while scheduling periodic and sporadic tasks. Specifically, the research: 1) specifies the physical environment and application; 2) describes local and global scheduling schemes for scheduling critical and non-critical tasks; and 3) evaluates the performance of the system and determines the cause of deadline failures by measuring the CPU utilization of the executor processors of each subsystem and identifying tasks with conflicting deadlines (a major factor which contributes to deadline failure). Due to space limitation, this paper provides only some insights to the above objectives. The detailed results can be found in [1J -[3J.

For the last two decades, different aspects of real time systems, particularly tasks scheduling [7], [10] have been studied extensively. More sophisticated algorithms have been presented to handle periodic and sporadic tasks using multiprocessor [9], [5] or distributed [8], systems. The importance of criticalness has been taken into consideration by some other researchers [4].

Most of the current scheduling algorithms are based on worst-case execution time rather than Pure Execution Time (PET). To find more precise information on the PET, Haban and Shin have introduced a real-time monitor [6]. In their approach after the first time that the system completed a task, its accurate execution time can be obtained and reported to the host. This approach is quite feasible for periodic tasks. Our methodology for scheduling critical and non-critical (could be periodic or sporadic) tasks is based upon consideration of worst-case execution time and utilization of a safety-time that is added to the execution time whenever it is possible. An enhanced three-phase local scheduler along with a global scheduler have been applied in scheduling local and remote tasks, respectively [2].

div.head: II. SYSTEM SPECIFICATION
div.p: As a part of a larger project, this model must support an Autonomous Multi-Robotics System (AMRS) which was initiated at University of Wyoming in 1990. The mission of the AMRS project is to provide an environment in which each individual robot can be trained and monitored to perform a set of complex tasks. Further, a robot must be able to transfer its knowledge or provide services to the other robots using a specified control mechanism.

The system is composed of a transputer based machine consisting of a T4 type and sixteen Ts type transputers. Presently, a 486 based machine equipped with a B004 board containing a T4 processor is functioning as the user interface unit. Two boards of types B012 are utilized by Tg' s processors. Each transputer consists of two mega bytes memory and four links (LQ -L4). The entire set of sixteen processors is divided into four homogeneous subsystems. Within each subsystem, four Tg processors are identified based on upon the assigned tasks termed as Executor (EX), Tasks Generator (TG), Local Scheduler (LS), and Global Scheduler (GS). Figure 1 shows the structure of a subsystem. At this stage of design, we like to make the target system independent of a particular type of robot. Thus, in addition to data manipulation and monitoring, the EX processor of each subsystem must simulate the behavior of the robot in executing the assigned task.

However, we left the link Lo of each of these processors free for future robot installation. Once the robot is installed, the EX will be assigned only to manipulate the data and monitor the corresponding robot. The TG processor communicates with the EX to collect the information on changes in the environment, generates tasks using predefined functions, and send them to the LS processor. The LS processor schedules the requested tasks and send them to the EX for execution. During the execution, the EX will monitor the sequence of actions taken by the robot. The GS is functioning as a global scheduler. Via a provided communication mechanism, it receives locally rejected tasks from the LS and schedules them for remote execution. Further, the GS provides facilities for the requests that are sent by the other subsystems.

The system requires three levels of communications. At the first level of communication, we must establish a mechanism between the system and the interface unit. The TG of one subsystem is assigned to send the result of computations of all the subsystems to and receive commands from the interface unit, respectively. The second level of communication requires a mechanism to transmit locally rejected tasks and receive remote tasks. Since the GS of each subsystem consists of three links to its neighbors, the links have been utilized to meet the requirements of the second level of communication. The third level of communication should be established among the logical elements within a subsystem. In addition to its task scheduling job, the LS of each subsystem is responsible for communication among the GS, TG, and the EX within the corresponding subsystem.

div.head: Tasks Scheduling Scheme
div.p: A distributed scheduling scheme is often divided into a local and a global scheduler. In most hard real time systems, the objective of developing a local task scheduler is to guarantee a maximum number of unpredictable critical tasks locally. Unfortunately, while a task's deadline is known at the arrival time, its computation time can only be estimated based upon static characteristics or previously observed behavior. Using such an estimation may cause a deadline failure [AlSu 90]. To alleviate this problem, we introduced a three-phase scheduling scheme which makes use of the idea of safety time, a factor that was added to the worstcase computation time of each task whenever the deadline on newly arrived task and the status of the scheduled tasks allow.

The success of scheduling a new task depends on its deadline, its worst-case computation time, and the current status of scheduled tasks. The current status of each scheduled task is stored in a scheduled list as S-LIST. This list is defined as 3-tuple S = < T, STF, S > where T is a set of tasks, STF is a set of safety time factors, and S is a set of empty slots. The complete details of the three-phase tasks scheduling algorithm can be found in [1] and [ 2].

div.head: Global Tasks Scheduler
div.p: The objective of developing a global scheduler is to provide facilities for scheduling locally rejected tasks. According to the three-phase local scheduling scheme, the tasks arc stored in the S-LIST (list of scheduled tasks) in the ascending order of their starting times. When the local scheduler is operating in phase-1 or phase-2, there may be an available time which can be utilized to schedule a remote task. The procedure for scheduling a remote task is different from the local task scheduler in a sense that the local scheduler has no control over the arrival time of a new task. On the other hand, in global scheduling schemes we try to control the arrival time of the remote tasks by sending a Remote Service Signal (RSS) from the LS to the GS processor. The GS then informs the other subsystems of an available time.

An RSS contains information on the available time, AVT, the starting time of the available time, ST.AVT, and the time period that resources can be held, th■ This information should be sufficient for a remote subsystem to make its decision in sending a task.

To prevent the LS from sending an unnecessary number of signals and reducing overhead, two system parameters are defined: Available Time Threshold (ATT) and Look Ahead Threshold (LAT). The ATT determines an available time slot that is large enough t o accommodate a remote task. The value of LAT determines how far we should look at the future within the S-LIST to find a valid available time.

It should be noted that when ITI = 0, the value LAT and ATT are both zero. That is, the local scheduler should immediately send an RSS to the GS. Further, the search for an available time should commence from the DT] and continue toward the t c . In this way, if an available time is found, there will be enough time to communicate with the other subsystems and schedule a remote task before the available time is expired. Finally, since there is no commitment from the remote subsystems in utilizing the available time, a holding time period, t h , is defined to prevent the LS from a pending state. Communication time between involved processors determines the value of t^.

During the operation, the GS can be in one of three states: scheduling , serving, or requesting state. The GS is in the scheduling state when a locally rejected task arrives from the LS of a remote subsystem. At this moment, the arrived task will be inserted onto the global queue within the GS according to the task's criticalness and deadline. Thus, at any given time, the tasks are stored in the global queue in the descending order of their criticalness.

When an RSS signal from the LS arrives, the global scheduler changes its state to the serving state. Then, it communicates with the other GSs one at a time to inform them that there is an available time in the S-LIST. This interaction will continue until a remote task has arrived, the GS receives a message that there is not a suitable remote task available, or the th expires. If the GS receives a remote request, it will send to the LS for further consideration. Otherwise, it informs the LS that there is no remote request.

The GS changes its state into the requesting state when there is a task which must be scheduled using remote resources. This state is initiated by an RSS from other subsystems. Once the GS is in the requesting state, it searches its global queue for a suitable task according to the AVT, and ST.AVT. After searching, either a global task or a rejected signal is returned to the subsystem which has offered remote service. Of course, before sending a global task, the GS has to verify that the th has not expired.

For scheduling locally rejected tasks and offering local resources to remote subsystems, a global process and four agents are provided. The combination of the global process, the monitor, and agents (see Figure 2), facilitates the GS with concurrent processes to provide services to the other subsystems and the LS.

div.head: III. PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS
div.p: The ability of a system to schedule different classes of tasks is highly dependent on the arrival rate and characteristics of the requested tasks such as deadlines. That is, during a specific time interval, Ti (system processing cycle), we may have a low arrival rate, but tasks may have deadline conflicts. As a result, more tasks may be rejected. On the other hand, we may have a high arrival rate of tasks that have no conflicts in terms of deadlines and the execution times. Thus, in an unpredictable environment, that there is no sufficient information on characteristics of the incoming tasks. The ability of the system in scheduling requested tasks must be measured in terms of the number of scheduled tasks in conjunction with the CPU utilization rate.

In light of the above discussion, we established two classes of experiments referred to as Class-1 and Class-2 experimental models. The suggested models are implemented using Occam language and INMOS transputer-based machine.

In Class-1 we consider the case in which the arrival rates of critical and non-critical sporadic tasks are variant. That is, all four subsystems through their TG processors generate a variant number of critical and non critical sporadic tasks in every given time interval. As these results indicate, the system is capable of completing and guaranteeing 82.9 percent of critical tasks and 69.7 percent of non-critical tasks generated by all subsystems. To understand the cause of the 14.8 percent rejected critical tasks, we looked at three major factors ; CPU utilization, deadline conflicting rate, and the arrival rate. Our findings indicate that during the entire period of the experiment, all four EX processors have been utilized more than 96.7 percent.

Further investigation into conflicting deadline issue indicates that out of 19 (14.8 %) rejected critical tasks 12 (9.3 %) had deadline conflicts. This shows that even with 100 percent CPU utilization of all EX processors, we would have about 9 and 20 percent of the critical and non-critical tasks rejected, respectively. Before making a final conclusion and providing an alternative, we must look at the significance of the variation in arrival rate factor.

In Class-2 we investigate the effect of arrival rate in the performance of the entire system. The same procedure as in Class-1 was applied. However, this time all four subsystems are generating & fixed number of tasks at any given time interval. The results show that the system is capable of scheduling about 84 percent of the total critical tasks using local resources. The rate of non-critical tasks that are guaranteed is about 72 percent. In this case the CPU utilization of the EX processors is between 97.3 to 98.7 percent.

According to the result of experiment, in each case all EX processors have been utilized more than 97 percent, and about 83.5 percent of critical tasks have been guaranteed to meet their deadlines. This observation indicates mat the schedulability of our model will not be affected by extreme variations in arrival rate.

With an average of 97 percent use of computational power in Class-1 and Class-2, about 13.6 percent of the critical tasks are still missing their deadlines (are rejected). The major reason for this undesirable situation is mat the majority of these rejected tasks (63%) have conflicting deadlines. Using arrival rate and conflicting deadlines in conjunction with the CPU utilization rate, one can determine computational power (number of processors) required to meet the demand of application. In our system, an alternative would be to monitor the processors which are dedicated to the global and local schedulers and utilize their idle times. However, interrupts and delays handling are essential to this approach.
